passage:
Madhuri: Mum told the whole wedding hall I'm "about to be a director" 😅
Gurpreet: Aren't you up for the team lead role?
Madhuri: Team lead. Maybe. Not even confirmed.
Gurpreet: Did you tell her that?
Madhuri: How? Her face was glowing. Papa is already ordering sweets 🥺
Gurpreet: You love that they're proud though.
Madhuri: I do!! It also makes my stomach hurt. What if it doesn't come through?
Gurpreet: Then they're still your mum and papa.
Madhuri: True. I should say it plainly tonight.
Gurpreet: Start with "I'm happy you're proud, and it isn't confirmed yet."
Madhuri: Okay. Will tell you how it goes ❤️

qa.q: What did Madhuri's mum tell the whole wedding hall?
qa.a: She said Madhuri was about to be a director.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Madhuri describe about the family's pride?
qa.a: Madhuri feels warm and glad that they are proud but also anxious, since the stomach hurts at the thought of the role not coming through.

qa.q: What could Madhuri say to the parents tonight?
qa.a: Madhuri could say plainly that being glad they are proud goes together with the role not being confirmed yet, as Gurpreet suggests.

qa.q: How might Madhuri's mum be feeling as she tells everyone?
qa.a: Her face was glowing, so she is probably full of joy and pride in her child, without realising the pressure it creates.

grounding: Family boasts about Madhuri to relatives; Madhuri feels warm and pressured, and plans to set expectations honestly.

passage: Since Sonali's dairy cooperative won the district award, her phone had not stopped. The man from the feed shop, who had never returned her calls, suddenly said, "Madam, you are a genius," and asked if she could find his brother a job at the cooperative. A distant cousin praised her at the bus stand and asked for a word with the officer. Sonali smiled and said thank you each time. That evening at Saurabh's tea stall she counted: seven compliments, five favours, and only two of these people had come when her cows fell sick last year. Saurabh, wiping the counter, said, "You're not wrong to notice. And for the record, the milk-testing form you filled last week had a mistake." It stung. She also felt oddly grateful.

qa.q: How many compliments and favours did Sonali count that evening?
qa.a: She counted seven compliments and five favours.

qa.q: What did Sonali notice about the new praise, and how did she feel about Saurabh's remark?
qa.a: She noticed that much of the praise came with a request from people who were absent last year, and she felt stung by Saurabh's correction yet oddly grateful for the honesty.

qa.q: What could Sonali do about the flood of praise and requests?
qa.a: Keep thanking people politely while checking whether they were around before, and keep close truthful friends like Saurabh who tell her when she is wrong.

qa.q: How might the man from the feed shop see his request?
qa.a: He may see it as ordinary asking of someone newly successful, though calling her a genius after ignoring her calls suggests he wants something.

grounding: Sudden praise brings favour requests; Sonali notices the pattern, thanks people, checks who was around before, and values a truthful friend.

passage:
Avni: They made me project lead today. I keep thinking they'll find out I don't know what I'm doing.
Jomon: You built the whole payment module.
Avni: With a lot of googling and Priya fixing my bugs.
Jomon: Everyone googles. You know that, right?
Avni: 😔 I know. It doesn't feel true at 1 a.m.
Jomon: Do you have a list of what you shipped this year?
Avni: There's a list?
Jomon: Make one. And ask your manager for feedback. A real question, like "what should I do better?"
Avni: Scary. But okay. I'll ask on Monday.
Jomon: And it's fine to say "I don't know yet" in meetings.
Avni: 🙂 Fine. Thank you.

qa.q: Which module did Avni build?
qa.a: Avni built the whole payment module.

qa.q: What is Avni afraid of after being made project lead?
qa.a: Avni fears being found out as not knowing what Avni is doing, a fear that feels strongest at 1 a.m.

qa.q: What steps does Jomon suggest to handle the feeling?
qa.a: Keep a list of what Avni shipped this year, ask the manager a real question about what to do better, and be willing to say "I don't know yet" in meetings.

qa.q: How does Jomon seem to see Avni's abilities?
qa.a: Jomon sees real achievement, pointing to the payment module and noting that everyone googles, and treats the doubt as common rather than as proof of fraud.

grounding: Success brings impostor fear; a friend points to the record of achievements, suggests asking for feedback and says not-knowing is fine.

passage: When the panchayat clerk announced that the school-book printing order had gone to Arohi's press, Hansa felt her jaw set. Two years in the same lane, and Arohi always seemed to get the luck. On the bus home she muttered to the conductor that Arohi must have greased somebody, then stopped, hearing herself. Nobody had said any such thing. The next morning she went to the clerk instead and asked, politely, why her bid had not been chosen. "The sample page and the delivery date," he said. "Arohi printed a sample overnight and brought it." Hansa looked at her own quote folder, all price and no sample. She wrote in her notebook: bring a sample, promise a date, keep it. Then she walked down the lane and, without gushing, told Arohi congratulations.

qa.q: Why did the panchayat clerk say Hansa's bid was not chosen?
qa.a: He said it came down to the sample page and the delivery date, since Arohi printed a sample overnight and brought it.

qa.q: What did Hansa realise when she heard herself muttering on the bus?
qa.a: She realised her envy was making her accuse Arohi of something nobody had said, so she stopped.

qa.q: What did Hansa do to turn envy into improvement?
qa.a: She asked the clerk why the bid was lost, noted to bring a sample and promise a date, and congratulated Arohi instead of bad-mouthing.

qa.q: How might Arohi see Hansa's congratulations?
qa.a: Arohi may be pleasantly surprised and see Hansa as a fair rival, especially since Hansa's grumbling on the bus never reached Arohi.

grounding: Hansa loses a bid and feels envy of the rival, then asks what the rival did better, plans to improve and does not run the rival down.

passage: Mentor's note, Friday review. Minakshi runs a small school-uniform business, and Bhavna's unit across town has won two school contracts in a row. Today Minakshi said aloud: "Bhavna's delivery has been on time every month. Ours slips." She did not blame luck or price. She said she had walked through Bhavna's stall at the school fair and noticed how every bundle is labelled by class. She will copy the labelling but keep her own stitching, which she thinks is better. She also mentioned that both firms run short of cloth in the monsoon and asked whether they could buy together. I told her Bhavna may say no, and that would be fine. I asked her to bring what she learns to next month's review. My impression: steady, not discouraged.

qa.q: How many school contracts in a row has Bhavna's unit won?
qa.a: Bhavna's unit has won two school contracts in a row.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's remark about delivery suggest she feels toward Bhavna's business?
qa.a: It suggests grounded respect: she admits that Bhavna's unit delivers on time and does not blame luck or price.

qa.q: How is Minakshi turning respect into a plan?
qa.a: She will copy the bundle labelling, keep her own stitching, and ask whether the two firms could buy cloth together in the monsoon.

qa.q: How might Bhavna respond to the idea of buying cloth together?
qa.a: Bhavna might say no, as the mentor points out, perhaps because Bhavna sees Minakshi's business as a competitor, and the mentor treats a refusal as acceptable.

grounding: Minakshi admits a competitor consistently delivers well, learns from them, competes fairly and considers collaboration where interests align.

passage: In the small office above a stationery shop, Aadhya pinned a printout to the whiteboard: a national chain had opened two shops in the district and was offering steep discounts to schools. The team of six read it in silence. Ira, the office manager, said, "Someone suggested we copy their price list and run down their quality to the principals. Just to hold on." Aadhya's stomach turned. "No," Aadhya said. "We'd lose the principals' trust in a week." She made a list: the five schools who call us by name, the hand-embroidered crests no chain does, the two staff who know every school's colours. "We call all five this week. Not to beg, to ask what they'd miss if we vanished." Ira wrote the names on the board.

qa.q: How many schools does Aadhya list as calling the firm by name?
qa.a: She lists five schools.

qa.q: What is Aadhya feeling when Ira relays the suggestion, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Aadhya feels uneasy and firm: the stomach turns and the quick "No" shows unwillingness to trade trust for short-term survival.

qa.q: What might Aadhya's firm do to protect what it does best?
qa.a: Call the five schools this week to ask what they would miss, and build on the hand-embroidered crests and the staff who know each school's colours. 👍

qa.q: How might a school principal see the firm if it ran down the chain's quality?
qa.a: The principal might lose trust in the firm, as Aadhya predicts within a week, and see it as desperate rather than reliable.

grounding: A smaller firm fears a bigger competitor, refuses unethical shortcuts, and focuses on niches, client relationships and key staff.

passage: Note from Darshan, staff welfare volunteer, after meeting Urmila on Tuesday. Urmila, 24, was passed over for a shift-supervisor post at the garment unit in favour of a newer colleague who is the owner's nephew, despite two years of better attendance records. She said the decision feels stone-hard and asked, "What's the point?" I did not promise anything. We went through what she has: her attendance sheets, the appointment email, and two co-workers willing to speak. I explained she could go to the unit's HR contact, the workers' union or the labour office, and that each takes time. I asked what fight she could afford: she may fight, wait for the next opening, or look elsewhere. She chose to file with HR and update her CV in parallel. I told her either choice is wise. Follow-up call next Tuesday.

qa.q: Who got the shift-supervisor post instead of Urmila?
qa.a: A newer colleague who is the owner's nephew got it.

qa.q: What does Urmila's question "What's the point?" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels helpless and stuck, as if the unfair decision cannot be moved.

qa.q: What steps did Darshan and Urmila go through?
qa.a: They listed her attendance sheets, the appointment email and two willing co-workers, named the routes (HR, union, labour office) and considered what fight she could afford.

qa.q: How might the newer colleague be seeing the promotion?
qa.a: The colleague may see it simply as an opportunity that was offered, without knowing how it looks to Urmila.

grounding: Urmila faces a seemingly immovable unfair decision; the note shows documenting, allies, formal routes and a choice about what fight to take.

passage:
Subject: I said something today

Dear Meghna,

You know Uday, the quiet one on the accounts desk? In today's review Mr Bose blamed Uday for the late report, though the delay was because sales sent the figures at 6 pm on Thursday. I have the email timestamps. My stomach was in knots. Then I put my hand up and said, "The figures reached us Thursday evening. I can show the emails." Two others nodded. Mr Bose went quiet, then said we would look at it again. I'm not sure it will fix anything, and I'm a bit scared I've marked myself. But silence would have told the whole floor that this is normal. Uday just said "thanks" in the pantry and looked at the floor. Wish me luck?

Pallavi

qa.q: What did Pallavi have that showed why the report was late?
qa.a: Pallavi had the email timestamps.

qa.q: Why is Pallavi scared even after speaking up?
qa.a: Pallavi worries that speaking up may have marked Pallavi as trouble, even though silence felt worse.

qa.q: What made Pallavi's speaking up safer than a bare accusation?
qa.a: Pallavi used facts, the emails with timestamps, and two others nodded in support.

qa.q: How might Uday have felt after Pallavi spoke?
qa.a: Probably relieved but awkward, since Uday said only "thanks" and looked at the floor. 🙂

grounding: Pallavi speaks up with facts when a coworker is blamed unfairly, aware of the risk and that silence makes injustice normal.

passage: After the meeting where the regional head announced that the delayed shipment was "Chinmay's oversight", Chinmay sat at his desk staring at nothing. The delay had been a warehouse fault, and he had emailed about it twice. Eshaan, two desks away, stayed back after everyone left and slid a printout onto his desk: the forwarded warnings, highlighted. "I sent the same thing to the regional head. Said I'd seen it myself." "They'll notice you," Chinmay said. "Let them." Chinmay swallowed. Next morning he told the head that any follow-up should come to him first, not Eshaan, since he had been the one on the account. At lunch he set a tiffin box on Eshaan's desk. "I owe you more than this." Eshaan grinned. "Then remember it."

qa.q: What was highlighted on the printout Eshaan gave Chinmay?
qa.a: The forwarded warnings were highlighted.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel about Eshaan's support, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Chinmay was moved and grateful: he swallowed, tried to shield Eshaan by asking that follow-up come to him first, and said he owed more than a tiffin box.

qa.q: How did Chinmay try to protect Eshaan and honour the debt?
qa.a: He asked the head to send any follow-up to him first and set a tiffin box on Eshaan's desk, saying he owed more than that.

qa.q: How might Eshaan see the risk taken?
qa.a: Eshaan seems aware of being noticed and says "Let them", which suggests standing up for fairness mattered more than staying safe.

grounding: A coworker stands by Chinmay after an unfair blame; he thanks them, tries to shield them from consequences and remembers the debt.

passage: Every Thursday at the community centre's free-meal kitchen, Nikita arrived first to wash the big steel pots. Tanuja, who managed the rota, teased her about it. "You could take the fun job, at the counter." Nikita smiled. "Two years ago I stood on the other side of that counter, new to the city and without a job. Someone slipped an extra roti onto my plate and never asked why." She touched the small idol on the shelf before rolling up her sleeves. "I thank God every morning, but I think I should thank people with my hands as well." Later she noticed a boy at the end of the queue, shy about asking for seconds, and quietly put a second helping beside him. She said nothing about it to anyone.

qa.q: What did Nikita do first every Thursday at the kitchen?
qa.a: She arrived first to wash the big steel pots.

qa.q: What does Nikita's remark about thanking people "with my hands" suggest she feels about her past?
qa.a: She is grateful for the person who once slipped her an extra roti when she had no job, and she expresses it by washing pots and serving without fuss.

qa.q: How does Nikita let gratitude show in daily life?
qa.a: Through generosity and humility: washing pots, serving, and quietly giving a shy boy a second helping.

qa.q: How might the boy in the queue see Nikita's second helping?
qa.a: He may feel quietly cared for and relieved not to have to ask, much as Nikita once was.

grounding: Nikita feels thanks for a past kindness and hard times survived, and lets gratitude show as generosity and humility, alongside her devotion.
